# Project Background & Data {background-color="#012169"}

::: {.notes}
Let me start with what we're analyzing and where the data comes from.
:::

---

## The NEPATEC 2.0 Dataset

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Source:** PNNL PermitAI — the most comprehensive
public NEPA database ever assembled

- [60,000+]{.highlight-stat} total federal projects
- [120,000+]{.highlight-stat} NEPA documents
- 60+ federal agencies
- Machine-readable full text (JSON)

**Clean Energy Universe:**

- ~25,000 initially tagged as clean energy
- [22,279]{.highlight-stat} after applying exclusion criteria
- Projects span 2000–2024

*This is the first analysis to systematically characterize
NEPA review patterns across the full clean energy portfolio.*
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![Energy type breakdown across all projects](../output/deliverable1/figures/00_energy_type_breakdown.png)

::: {.caption-text}
Clean energy: 37% | Fossil fuel: 18% | Other energy/infrastructure: 45%
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
NEPATEC 2.0 was assembled by PNNL as part of their PermitAI initiative. The key innovation is that it converted tens of thousands of PDF documents into machine-readable format with metadata tags. Before this dataset existed, there was no systematic way to study NEPA review patterns across agencies and technologies at this scale. The 22,279 number is our working clean energy universe after we applied deliberate exclusion criteria.
:::

---

## Defining Clean Energy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Clean Energy Tags** *(any 1 qualifies)*

| Tag Category |
|---|
| Renewable Energy Production |
| Electricity Transmission |
| Nuclear Technology |
| Carbon Capture & Sequestration |
| Utilities (electricity/gas) |
| Biomass / Biofuels |
| Battery / Energy Storage |
| Fuel Cells / Hydrogen |
| *...and 6 more* |

**Rule:** ≥1 clean energy tag **AND** no fossil fuel tags
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Fossil Fuel Tags** *(any 1 excludes)*

| Tag | Effect |
|---|---|
| Conventional Energy — Coal | Excluded |
| Conventional Energy — Land Oil & Gas | Excluded |
| Conventional Energy — Offshore Oil & Gas | Excluded |
| Conventional Energy — Rural Energy | Excluded |
| Pipelines (fossil fuel) | Excluded |

**Key exclusions applied to clean energy:**

1. Utilities-only + non-energy tags: **1,623 removed**
2. Military/Defense + Nuclear: **481 removed**
3. Nuclear + Waste Management: all but **34 retained**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The tagging system uses both document metadata and NLP on document titles and descriptions. The exclusions were carefully reviewed — without them, the "clean energy" category would have included nuclear weapons facilities and waste disposal. CATF staff reviewed samples from each exclusion category to validate the approach.
:::

# Deliverable 1 {background-color="#012169"}
## Clean Energy Project Landscape

::: {.notes}
D1 answers the foundational question: how are clean energy NEPA projects distributed across technologies, agencies, and geography?
:::

---

## Technology Distribution {.slide-label data-deliverable="D1"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Projects by technology type](../output/deliverable1/figures/01_clean_energy_bar_chart.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Technology breakdown by NEPA process](../output/deliverable1/figures/02_clean_energy_bar_by_process.png)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
**Utilities, Electricity Transmission, and Nuclear dominate.** Hydropower, Nuclear, and Wind show notably higher EA/EIS rates — reflecting larger environmental footprints or regulatory requirements.
:::

::: {.notes}
The left chart shows raw project counts by technology. The right shows the same data broken down by NEPA review process type (CE/EA/EIS). The dominance of CEs across most technologies reflects DOE's portfolio — large numbers of relatively small projects processed administratively. The higher EA/EIS rates for Hydro, Nuclear, and Wind are important for understanding where the most intensive NEPA review is concentrated.
:::

---

## Lead Agencies: DOE Dominates

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![Projects by department and NEPA process](../output/deliverable1/figures/02_departments.png)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-finding}
- **DOE: 81% of clean energy projects**
- DOE processes **96%** through Categorical Exclusions
- Interior: 17% of projects; more varied process mix
- Other agencies (USDA, Army Corps) have higher EA/EIS shares
:::

**Why DOE dominates:**

- Loan programs (DOE Loan Programs Office)
- Power Marketing Administrations (BPA, TVA, etc.)
- Grid modernization and R&D grants
- National Laboratory site operations
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
DOE's 81% share and 96% CE rate is a striking feature of the clean energy NEPA landscape. This concentration has policy implications — CE status means limited public review and shorter timelines. Interior's more varied mix reflects its land management mission where larger-footprint projects (utility-scale solar, wind farms on federal land) require EAs or EISs more often.
:::

---

## Geographic Distribution

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![Clean energy projects by state](../output/deliverable1/maps/09_state_choropleth.png)
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
**Top 5 States:**

1. South Carolina *(Savannah River Site)*
2. Washington
3. California
4. Idaho
5. Colorado

**County-Level Coverage:**

| Process | Coverage |
|---|---|
| All | 48% have county |
| CE | 46% |
| EA | 81% |
| EIS | 64% |

::: {.small-text}
~397 EA/EIS projects missing county data are
estimated **~99% recoverable** via reverse geocoding
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
South Carolina's dominance is an artifact of the Savannah River Site — a massive DOE nuclear facility that generates enormous NEPA review activity. Washington reflects Hanford and the Pacific Northwest. The county coverage gap for CEs is a data quality issue — CE documents often contain legal land descriptions rather than coordinates. The good news is this is almost entirely recoverable for the EA/EIS projects that matter most for policy analysis.
:::

## D1 Key Takeaways {background-color="#012169"}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em;"}

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Scale:** 22,279 clean energy projects — far more NEPA activity than previously documented
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**DOE dominance:** 81% of projects, 96% via CE — the clean energy permitting story is largely a DOE CE story
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Geography:** South Carolina leads due to one federal nuclear facility — important context when reading geographic distributions
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}

# Deliverable 2 {background-color="#012169"}
## Programmatic & Tiered Reviews

::: {.notes}
D2 asks: how many NEPA reviews are programmatic or tiered, and do these "efficient" review types actually deliver faster outcomes?
:::

---

## Programmatic & Tiered Reviews Are the Minority

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Review type distribution across EA/EIS](../output/deliverable2/figures/02_review_share.png)

::: {.callout-finding}
Only **35.5%** of EA/EIS clean energy projects
(1,503 of 4,231) are programmatic or tiered
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Top agencies for non-standard reviews](../output/deliverable2/figures/02_agency.png)

**BLM dominates** (50%+ of non-standard reviews)
reflecting its western land management mission

**Western state concentration:**
California, Nevada, Washington lead

*Detection method: title keyword matching +
regex extraction from first 60 document pages*
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The 35.5% figure is lower than many assume. BLM's dominance reflects how Resource Management Plans frequently serve as programmatic NEPA documents for subsequent site-specific actions. The detection methodology uses two-stage text analysis — not just metadata — which makes it more reliable but also means we may undercount in some cases.
:::

---

## Are Tiered Reviews Actually Faster?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![Duration by review type](../output/deliverable2/figures/02_duration.png)
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
**Median review durations:**

| Review Type | EA | EIS |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | 294 days | 1,042 days |
| Tiered | **380 days** | — |
| Programmatic | — | **924 days** |

::: {.callout-finding}
**Tiered EAs are *longer* than standard EAs.**
Programmatic EISs are modestly faster, but
the distribution overlap is substantial.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Caution:** Small sample for tiered EIS limits
conclusions about that category
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a counterintuitive finding that challenges the standard efficiency argument for tiering. The assumption is that establishing a programmatic framework upfront saves time on site-specific reviews. In practice, tiered EAs still require full site-specific analysis, coordination with the parent review, and often additional public comment periods. The duration distributions substantially overlap — tiering is not a reliable speed advantage.
:::

---

## D2 Key Takeaways {background-color="#012169"}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em;"}

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Prevalence:** Only 35.5% of EA/EIS projects use programmatic or tiered review — these are not the norm
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Speed:** Tiering does **not** reliably speed up environmental review — tiered EAs are actually *slower* than standard EAs
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Who uses them:** BLM drives more than half of non-standard reviews; western states dominate
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Policy implication:** Expanding tiering requirements alone will not accelerate permitting without addressing root causes of EA/EIS duration
:::

:::

# Deliverable 3 {background-color="#012169"}
## NEPA Process, Timelines & Generation Capacity

::: {.notes}
D3 is the most data-rich deliverable — how do CE, EA, and EIS compare on duration? How has NEPA activity changed over time? And what generation capacity is associated with each review type?
:::

---

## How Long Does NEPA Review Take?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![Timeline duration summary by process type](../output/deliverable3/figures/03_duration_summary_intervals_by_process.png)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**Median durations:**

- CE: [~1 month]{.highlight-stat}
- EA: [~14 months]{.highlight-stat}
- EIS: [~34 months (3 yrs)]{.highlight-stat}

**90th percentile:**

- EIS: [> 7.5 years]{.highlight-stat}

**Timeline completeness:**

| Process | Both Dates |
|---|---|
| CE | 30% |
| EA | 62% |
| EIS | 48% |

::: {.small-text}
*Dates extracted via custom BERT NLP pipeline
from document text*
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The 7.5-year 90th percentile for EIS is the number that drives the NEPA delay narrative in policy debates. But it's important to contextualize: this is the tail of the distribution, representing a small fraction of total reviews. The 34-month median is a more representative picture for EIS. Timeline completeness is low for CEs (30%) because CE documents are shorter and contain less temporal information — this is a data limitation, not necessarily a signal of missing reviews.
:::

---

## NEPA Activity Over Time

![Clean energy projects by NEPA decision year (2010–2024)](../output/deliverable3/figures/03_projects_by_year.png)

::: {.callout-finding}
**CE peaked in 2010** (ARRA stimulus) and again in **2023**. The IRA/BIL investment surge (2022) has not yet fully appeared — projects initiated in 2022–2023 will decide in 2024–2026.
:::

::: {.notes}
The 2010 ARRA peak is a direct signal of the Recovery Act flowing through federal agencies as CE-processed grants and loans. The 2023 uptick reflects IRA and BIL early activity — but because CE is fast and EIS is slow, we're likely seeing IRA projects that were initiated quickly and completed. The larger IRA/BIL cohort of EAs and EISs initiated in 2022–2024 won't show up in completion data until later years.
:::

---

## Generation Capacity by Review Process

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Capacity distribution by process type (stacked)](../output/deliverable3/figures/05_capacity_by_process.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Capacity distribution violin and boxplot](../output/deliverable3/figures/06_capacity_distribution_violin_box.png)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
**EIS median: [538 MW]{.highlight-stat}** &nbsp;|&nbsp; **EA median: [60 MW]{.highlight-stat}** &nbsp;|&nbsp; **CE median: [1.2 MW]{.highlight-stat}**
Review intensity is broadly proportional to project scale — consistent with NEPA's risk-proportional design.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a reassuring finding from a policy perspective: the review process is broadly calibrated to project size. Utility-scale projects (500+ MW) predominantly receive EIS reviews. The tail of CE projects with higher capacity warrants further investigation — are these genuinely low-impact large projects, or candidates for review of CE category appropriateness? Capacity data coverage is much higher for EIS (81%) than CE (8%), so CE statistics are less reliable.
:::

---

## D3 Key Takeaways {background-color="#012169"}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em;"}

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Scale matters:** CE = 1 month, EA = 14 months, EIS = 3 years median — the difference is real and large
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Long tail:** 10% of EIS reviews take more than 7.5 years — these outliers drive the NEPA delay narrative but are not typical
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Stimulus signal:** ARRA (2010) and IRA/BIL (2022–) are visible in the data; the full IRA cohort is still working through the pipeline
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Proportionality:** Review intensity broadly matches project scale — the largest projects (500+ MW) appropriately receive EIS-level review
:::

:::

The state connection map shows which corridors are most active — these are the infrastructure arteries of the clean energy transition.
:::

## Multi-Agency Collaboration

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Department collaboration hub scores](../output/deliverable4/figures/fig_department_collaboration_hubs.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The bridge score is a network centrality measure — DOE's score of 26 means it appears as a co-agency in a far wider range of multi-agency reviews than any other department. The 89% EIS rate for multi-agency projects is expected — these are the largest, most complex projects that affect multiple jurisdictions and resource areas.
:::

# Deliverable 5 {background-color="#012169"}
## Document Length & Fiscal Responsibility Act Impact

::: {.notes}
D5 asks: did the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023's page limits actually change how long NEPA documents are? This is directly relevant to current policy debates about permitting reform.
:::

---

## The FRA 2023 Page Limits

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Fiscal Responsibility Act (June 2023) established:**

| Document | Standard Limit | Complex Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Environmental Assessment | **75 pages** | — |
| Environmental Impact Statement | **150 pages** | **300 pages** |

**Regulatory "page" definition** *(40 C.F.R. § 1508.1(bb))*:

> Body word count ÷ 500
> *Excludes:* maps, figures, graphs, tables, appendices, citations

::: {.callout-finding}
This analysis uses **regulatory pages** to match the statutory definition — not raw PDF page counts, which overstate document length by 45–55% for EAs and 20–30% for EISs due to bundled appendices.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Why this matters:**

- FRA is among the most significant NEPA reforms in decades
- Page limits were intended to force concise, focused analysis
- Compliance depends heavily on how "pages" are counted
- Waivers and "extraordinary complexity" exceptions complicate assessment

**Our approach:**

- Final EA/EIS only (drafts excluded)
- Clean energy projects with complete timelines
- Post-FRA = decision date ≥ June 3, 2023
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The methodological choice to use regulatory pages is critical. If we used raw PDF pages, compliance rates would appear much lower and would be misleading — a 200-page document with 100 pages of appendices might have only 50 regulatory pages and be fully compliant. The body-word-count method is the correct interpretation of the statutory definition, but it requires detecting appendix boundaries in OCR text, which introduces some error.
:::

---

## Document Length Trends Over Time

![Individual project page counts and 3-month rolling average (2010–2024)](../output/deliverable5/figures/05_pages_over_time.png)

::: {.callout-finding}
**Document lengths were already declining before FRA.** The rolling average trend predates June 2023. Post-FRA mean EA fell ~22%, EIS fell ~25% — but causation is uncertain.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Small post-FRA sample:** Only 33 EAs and 42 EISs completed after June 2023 — limit strong causal claims.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most important cautionary finding in D5. The declining trend is real, but it appears to have started before FRA. Possible explanations: informal agency compliance with anticipated limits, simpler projects entering the pipeline, or general efficiency improvements. We cannot use this data alone to establish that FRA caused the decline. The post-FRA sample is also small — as more post-FRA documents accumulate, this analysis will become more definitive.
:::

---

## Pre/Post FRA Comparison & Compliance

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Pre vs. Post FRA mean and median page counts](../output/deliverable5/figures/05_pages_pre_post_fra.png)

**Regulatory page medians:**

| | Pre-FRA | Post-FRA | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| EA | 41 | **33** | −20% |
| EIS | 120 | **93** | −23% |
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![FRA compliance rates (post-FRA only)](../output/deliverable5/figures/05_fra_compliance.png)

**Compliance rates (post-FRA):**

- EA (75-page limit): [76%]{.highlight-stat} comply
- EIS (150-page limit): [27%]{.highlight-stat} comply
- EIS in 150–300 range: 48%

::: {.small-text}
*Compliance data lacks context: waivers,
"extraordinary complexity" exceptions,
and grandfathering are not distinguished*
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The 76% EA compliance is encouraging. The 27% EIS compliance for the 150-page limit looks bad, but note that 48% fall in the 150–300 range, which may qualify for the extraordinary complexity exception. Without document-by-document review, we can't distinguish which of these properly invoked the exception. The compliance picture for EIS may be more favorable than the 27% headline suggests. But 26% exceeding even 300 pages is notable — those projects are clearly out of compliance.
:::

---

## D5 Key Takeaways {background-color="#012169"}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em;"}

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Decline is real:** EA and EIS document lengths fell ~20–25% post-FRA — a meaningful reduction if it holds
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Causation is uncertain:** The downward trend preceded FRA; the law may have reinforced, not initiated, the decline
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**EA compliance is solid:** 76% of post-FRA EAs comply with the 75-page limit
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**EIS compliance is low:** Only 27% comply with the 150-page limit; many may qualify for the 300-page exception — but 26% exceed even that
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Watch this space:** The post-FRA sample (33 EAs, 42 EISs) is small — conclusions will strengthen as more post-FRA documents accumulate through 2025–2026
:::

:::

# Deliverable 6 {background-color="#012169"}
## Technology Deep Dives

::: {.notes}
D6 zooms into three specific technology areas: electricity transmission lines, geothermal energy, and pipelines — including the emerging carbon and hydrogen categories.
:::

---

## Electricity Transmission Lines

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Transmission projects and duration by length band](../output/deliverable6/figures/fig_transmission_length_bins.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Duration by action type](../output/deliverable6/figures/fig_transmission_duration_by_action.png)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
**151 projects** with extractable line lengths &nbsp;|&nbsp; Median **8 miles** &nbsp;|&nbsp; **55%** under 10 miles
Projects ≥100 miles take [6× longer]{.highlight-stat} than projects under 10 miles
:::

::: {.notes}
The 151 strict clean-energy transmission projects come from a 3-gate classification: electricity transmission tag, build-related language in title/description, and extractable line length ≥1 mile. The 38.5-day median across all transmission projects is driven by the many short, CE-processed upgrades and replacements. The 6x duration multiplier for 100+ mile lines is striking and has direct implications for the large-scale transmission buildout needed for the energy transition.
:::

---

## Geothermal Energy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Geothermal duration by development phase](../output/deliverable6/figures/fig_geothermal_phase_duration_boxplot.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Multi-phase project sequencing within projects](../output/deliverable6/figures/fig_geothermal_within_project_sequence.png)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
**914 NEPA actions** across **5 phases** &nbsp;|&nbsp; Drilling is most common and fastest &nbsp;|&nbsp; Exploration & multi-phase reviews are longest
**A single geothermal project may require multiple sequential NEPA reviews** — the within-project timeline is a multi-year permitting journey.
:::

::: {.notes}
Geothermal is unique because each phase of development — exploration, confirmation drilling, plant construction, operations — may trigger a separate NEPA review. The within-project sequencing figure shows how these phases chain together over time. This has a direct policy implication: the total NEPA burden for a geothermal project is the cumulative sum of multiple reviews, not just one. Streamlining geothermal permitting requires addressing this sequencing problem, not just making individual reviews faster.
:::

---

::: {.callout-finding}
**6,133 total pipeline NEPA actions** &nbsp;|&nbsp; Carbon pipelines have the longest median length &nbsp;|&nbsp; Natural gas provides the most statistically reliable baseline

The pipeline dataset includes natural gas, oil, carbon capture, and hydrogen categories. Oil and natural gas provide reliable baselines by count. The carbon and hydrogen categories are critically important for policy — carbon pipeline buildout is essential for CCS, and hydrogen pipelines are emerging — but the current data is too thin for strong statistical conclusions. This will improve as new projects enter the permitting system.

## D6 Key Takeaways {background-color="#012169"}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em;"}

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Transmission length = duration:** 100+ mile transmission lines take 6× longer than short lines — a critical constraint for large-scale grid buildout
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Geothermal phases:** A full geothermal development project requires multiple sequential NEPA reviews — streamlining requires addressing the whole lifecycle
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Carbon/hydrogen data is thin:** Only single-digit to low-double-digit projects have full data — findings are directional, not definitive
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Upgrades vs. new builds:** Most transmission NEPA activity is upgrades and replacements, not greenfield new construction — important context for buildout policy
:::

:::

[Full Deliverable 6 Report](../reports/deliverable06.html)

## Phase 1 Summary: Key Findings Across All Deliverables

::: {.incremental}
1. **Scale** — 22,279 clean energy projects documented; the NEPA clean energy portfolio is larger than previously understood
2. **DOE dominance** — 81% of projects, 96% via Categorical Exclusion; the permitting story is largely a DOE CE story
3. **Tiering doesn't automatically help** — programmatic/tiered reviews represent only 35% of EA/EIS and are not reliably faster
4. **Duration gradient is steep** — CE (~1 month) → EA (~14 months) → EIS (~3 years median, 7.5-year 90th pctile)
5. **Review matches scale** — EIS projects are genuinely large (median 538 MW); CE projects are genuinely small (median 1.2 MW)
6. **DOE is the multi-agency hub** — improving DOE-DOI-USDA coordination would have outsized impact on complex reviews
7. **FRA effect is real but uncertain** — document lengths fell ~20–25%; causation is not yet established; EIS compliance is low
8. **Technology matters** — transmission length predicts duration; geothermal requires multi-phase permitting; carbon/hydrogen data needs to grow
:::

::: {.notes}
These are the eight core findings from Phase 1. The incremental reveal allows the audience to focus on each one. Invite reactions after showing all eight — which is most surprising? Most actionable?
:::

## A3: Timeline Extraction Methodology

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Two-Stage Extraction Pipeline:**

1. **Date extraction** — identify all dates in document text with surrounding sentence context
2. **Date classification** — BERT sequence labeler assigns each date to:
   - Initiation (NOI, application received, scoping)
   - Review (draft publication, comment period)
   - Decision (ROD, FONSI, signature)
   - Other

**Timeline Selection Rules:**

- Decision date: prioritize strong signature/approval cues; avoid "expected" future dates
- Initiation date: prioritize formal trigger events (NOI > application > scoping)
- Fallback: use earliest review date as proxy initiation when no initiation found
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Known Limitations:**

::: {.callout-warning}
- **CE completeness (30%):** Short documents have less temporal information
- **EIS completeness (48%):** RODs often issued as separate documents, not linked in dataset
- **EA completeness (62%):** Best coverage; FONSIs typically included
- **Class imbalance:** Initiation dates are harder to classify than decision dates
:::

**Model:** Fine-tuned BERT (bert-base-uncased) trained on manually annotated NEPA document sentences
:::
:::

## A5: Geothermal Phase Distribution

![Geothermal NEPA actions by development phase](../output/deliverable6/figures/fig_geothermal_phase_distribution.png)

::: {.small-text}
Phase classification uses regex pattern matching on project title and description text. Projects matching keywords from 2+ phase categories are classified as "multi-phase." Projects with no keyword match fall back to process type (CE → drilling; EA/EIS → exploration).
:::

![Pipeline length vs. NEPA duration by pipeline type](../output/deliverable6/figures/fig_pipeline_length_vs_duration.png)

::: {.small-text}
Modest positive correlation between pipeline length and NEPA duration across all pipeline types. High variance in both dimensions. Natural gas provides the most statistically reliable trend line. Carbon and hydrogen samples (8 and 4 projects respectively) are too small for regression inference.
:::

## A7: FRA Regulatory vs. Raw Pages Methodology

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Regulatory Page Calculation:**

1. Extract body text from OCR'd PDF
2. Detect appendix boundaries using section-header patterns:
   - "Appendix [A-Z]", "References", "Bibliography", "List of Preparers", etc.
3. Count words in body text (pre-appendix)
4. Regulatory pages = body word count ÷ 500

**Why this differs from raw page count:**

- Raw pages include all embedded maps, figures, appendices
- EAs: regulatory ≈ 45–55% of raw pages
- EISs: regulatory ≈ 70–80% of raw pages
- Raw-page compliance would show much lower rates
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Known edge cases:**

::: {.callout-warning}
- **OCR errors:** Scanned legacy documents may have NULL word counts
- **Non-standard headers:** Some appendices use non-standard naming and may not be detected
- **Table-heavy documents:** ~5% of cases show regulatory pages exceeding raw pages (OCR text extraction artifact)
- **Waivers and exceptions:** Cannot distinguish properly invoked "extraordinary complexity" exceptions from non-compliant documents
:::
:::
:::
